# Sanitising the microscope {#sec-sanitising}

A microscope going into an incubator is usually cleaned first. These are the
methods Etaluma recommends.

## Wiping down with alcohol {#sec-alcohol}

Ethanol and isopropanol are the two alcohols most used for their biocidal
action. They disrupt cell membranes, dissolve lipids and denature proteins,
and these processes need water, so the alcohol must be diluted to 60% to 90%
in water to work (typically 70%, by volume). They act on lipid-containing
viruses and a broad range of bacteria, but not on spore-forming bacteria.
They evaporate fast, so a long contact time is hard to reach without
immersion. Alcohols are generally regarded as non-corrosive.

## Wiping down with bleach {#sec-bleach}

Chlorine compounds are inexpensive, fast-acting disinfectants with a broad
antimicrobial range. Hypochlorites, the most used, come as liquids (sodium
hypochlorite, as in household bleach) and solids (calcium hypochlorite,
sodium dichloroisocyanurate). Household bleach holds 5.25% available
chlorine, 52,500 ppm. It is a strong oxidiser and loses strength quickly, so
make it fresh and use it the day it is made.

## Hydrogen peroxide vapour (HPV) {#sec-hpv}

Hydrogen peroxide vapour removes biological agents from equipment surfaces,
including ones hard to sterilise otherwise. Because a vapour reaches every
surface, it is used for pass-through chambers and for devices in hospitals
and manufacturing.

HPV decontaminates a CO~2~ incubator without heat, which spares a research
lab costly down time. A seven-minute HPV fog circulated by the incubator's
blower, followed by narrow-band ultraviolet light, disinfects effectively.
It reaches every wall, shelf, reservoir, air plenum, sensor and other
interior part, and leaves only a little sterile water behind.
